since time immemorial in southern Louisiana along the Gulf Coast from the Mississippi River Delta West to the Texas border.}}) is a [[language isolate]] historically spoken by the [[Chitimacha]] people of [[Louisiana]], United States. It became extinct in 1940 with the death of the last fluent speaker, Delphine Ducloux. Although no longer spoken, it is fairly extensively documented in the early 20th-century work (mostly unpublished) of [[linguist]]s [[Morris Swadesh]]{{Cite journal |last=Swadesh |first=Morris |author-link=Morris Swadesh |jstor=1262876 |title=Sociologic Notes on Obsolescent Languages |journal=[[International Journal of American Linguistics]] |volume=14 |issue=4 |year=1948 |pages=226–235 |doi=10.1086/464009 |s2cid=144458026}}{{Cite journal |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=345–362 |last=Swadesh |first=M. |title=The phonetics of Chitimacha |journal=Language |year=1934 |doi=10.2307/409490 |jstor=409490}} and [[John R. Swanton]]. Swadesh in particular wrote a full grammar and dictionary, and collected numerous texts from the last two speakers, although none of this is published. [[Language revitalization]] efforts are underway to teach the language to a new generation of speakers.{{Cite web |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RDzFPDuadek |title=YouTube – Chitimacha Language Episode – Finding Our Talk 3 |work=youtube.com |access-date=January 26, 2010 }}{{cbignore}}{{Dead Youtube links|date=February 2022}}{{Cite web | title = Press Release, Media Room, Rosetta Stone | access-date = 2012-08-26 | url = http://pr.rosettastone.com/phoenix.zhtml?c=228009&p=irol-newsArticle&ID=1273965&highlight | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171020213700/http://pr.rosettastone.com/phoenix.zhtml?c=228009&p=irol-newsArticle&ID=1273965&highlight | archive-date = 2017-10-20 | url-status = dead }}{{Cite web | author = Larry Abramson (Director) | title = Software Company Helps Revive 'Sleeping' Language | work = All Things Considered - NPR | access-date = 2012-08-26 | date = 2010-02-02 | url = https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=123220585 }} Tribal members have received [[Rosetta Stone (software)|Rosetta Stone]] software for learning the language. As of 2015, a new Chitimacha dictionary is in preparation, and classes are being taught on the Chitimacha reservation.{{Cite web|title = The Successful Revival of the Chitimacha Language|url = http://languagemagazine.com/?p=124218|access-date = 2015-10-03|website = Language Magazine|date = August 2015|last = Heflin|first = Judy}} ==Classification== Chitimacha, though conventionally regarded as a language isolate, has recently been proposed to be related to, or a member of, the proposed [[Totozoquean languages|Totozoquean language family]].{{Cite journal |title=Chitimacha: A Mesoamerican language in the Lower Mississippi valley |first1=Cecil H. |last1=Brown |first2=Søren |last2=Wichmann |first3=David |last3=Beck |year=2014 |journal=International Journal of American Linguistics |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=425–474 |doi=10.1086/677911 |s2cid=145538166 }} These proposals have not been accepted by the wider linguistic community.{{Citation |last=Campbell |first=Lyle |title=Distant Linguistic Relationships |date=2024-06-25 |work=The Indigenous Languages of the Americas |pages=339–387 |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/57386/chapter/464723041 |access-date=2025-11-10 |edition=1 |publisher=Oxford University PressNew York |language=en |doi=10.1093/oso/9780197673461.003.0006 |isbn=978-0-19-767346-1|url-access=subscription }} An automated computational analysis ([[Automated Similarity Judgment Program|ASJP]] 4) by Müller et al. (2013) found lexical similarities between Chitimacha, [[Huave language|Huave]], and [[Totozoquean languages|Totozoquean]].{{cite web |first1=André |last1=Müller |first2=Viveka |last2=Velupillai |first3=Søren |last3=Wichmann |first4=Cecil H. |last4=Brown |first5=Eric W. |last5=Holman |first6=Sebastian |last6=Sauppe |first7=Pamela |last7=Brown |first8=Harald |last8=Hammarström |first9=Oleg |last9=Belyaev |first10=Johann-Mattis |last10=List |first11=Dik |last11=Bakker |first12=Dmitri |last12=Egorov |first13=Matthias |last13=Urban |first14=Robert |last14=Mailhammer |first15=Matthew S. |last15=Dryer |first16=Evgenia |last16=Korovina |first17=David |last17=Beck |first18=Helen |last18=Geyer |first19=Pattie |last19=Epps |first20=Anthony |last20=Grant |first21=Pilar |last21=Valenzuela |display-authors=3 |url=https://asjp.clld.org/static/WorldLanguageTree-004.zip |title=ASJP World Language Trees of Lexical Similarity |version=4 |date=October 2013}} However, since the analysis was automatically generated, the grouping could be either due to mutual lexical borrowing or genetic inheritance. Chitimacha distinguishes several word classes: verbs, nouns, adjectives (verbal and nominal), quantifiers, demonstratives. Swadesh (1946) states that the remaining word classes are hard to distinguish but may be divided "into proclitics, postclitics, and independent particles". Chitimacha has auxiliaries which are inflected for tense, aspect and mood, such as ''to be''. Polar interrogatives may be marked with a final falling intonation and a clause final post-position. Chitimacha does not appear to have adopted any grammatical features from their interactions with the French, Spanish or Americans.{{cite book |first=Morris |last=Swadesh |year=1946 |chapter=Chitimach |editor-last=Hoijer |editor-first=Harry |title=Linguistic structures of native America |pages=312–336 |location=New York |publisher=Viking Fund}} ===Pronouns=== Verbs are inflected for person and number of the subject. Ambiguity may be avoided by the use of the personal pronouns (shown in the table below), but sentences without personal pronouns are common. There is no [[Grammatical gender|gender]] in the personal pronouns and verbal indexes. Pronouns cannot be preceded by a possessive unlike nouns. === Nouns === There are definite [[Article (grammar)|articles]] in Chitimacha.{{cite thesis |first=David V. |last=Kaufman |year=2014 |title=The Lower Mississippi Valley as a Language Area |type=Doctoral dissertation |publisher=University of Kansas}} Nouns are mostly uninflected; there are only approximately 30 nouns (mostly kinship or referring to persons) which distinguish a singular or plural form through a plural suffix or other formations. Nouns are free, or may be possessed by juxtaposing the possessor and the possessed noun. :{{lang|ctm|ʔiš ʔinž̹i}} = my father ("I father") :{{lang|ctm|was ʔasi ʔinž̹i}} = that man's father ("that man
